description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

In this section (maximum 1000 words), please provide a global overview of the project progress **per output**. To what extent have they been achieved? Comment on the activities that have taken place and the most important milestones.

actual.value:
1. Increased capacity to work with flying sensor and satellite-derived data: The project has made significant progress in enhancing the capacity of the participants to work with flying sensor and satellite-derived data. The online training courses conducted by FutureWater provided a comprehensive understanding of the applications, processing, and interpretation of aerial imagery. The participants, numbering over 260, gained valuable knowledge and skills in utilizing flying sensors, such as drones, for agricultural systems. The training covered aspects like safety management, controlling drones in manual and automatic modes, image processing techniques including generating orthomosaics and crop stress maps, as well as georeferencing. These training activities have laid a strong foundation for the participants to effectively work with flying sensors and satellite-derived data. 2. Increased capacity to access and work with open-access geodata: The project has also focused on enhancing the capacity of the participants to access and work with open-access geodata. The training courses provided by FutureWater emphasized the use of tools for imagery viewing and reporting, enabling participants to effectively utilize open-access geodata in their work. Additionally, the utilization of WaPOR, a remotely sensed derived data platform, was covered in the training, providing participants with the necessary skills to access and analyze geospatial data related to water management and agricultural performance. By familiarizing the participants with open-access geodata and providing them with the tools and knowledge to work with such data, the project has contributed to increasing their capacity in this area. 3. Enhanced uptake of flying sensors and satellite-derived data in daily work: The project has aimed to facilitate the enhanced uptake of flying sensors and satellite-derived data in the daily work of the participants. The training sessions, both online and in-country, have equipped the participants with practical skills and knowledge that can be directly applied in their work. By focusing on the use of drones in agriculture, the project has provided participants with the necessary piloting skills and image processing techniques to effectively utilize flying sensors in their agricultural systems. The emphasis on interpreting the imagery captured by flying sensors has further enhanced the participants' ability to analyze and utilize satellite-derived data for addressing agricultural and water-related challenges. By training staff with lecturing responsibilities, the project has also ensured the transfer of these skills to students, thereby extending the impact of the training beyond the participants themselves. Approximately 50% of the participants have indicated to have applied their newly acquired knowledge in their daily work already and the rest envision to do this in the short term.
Overall, the project has made significant progress in achieving its outputs. The capacity of the participants to work with flying sensor and satellite-derived data has been greatly increased through the comprehensive training courses. The participants have gained valuable skills in piloting drones, processing aerial imagery, and accessing open-access geodata. These skills are directly applicable to their daily work and will contribute to improved agricultural and water management practices. The project has successfully enhanced the uptake of flying sensors and satellite-derived data in the participants' work, with a particular focus on the agricultural sector. The training activities and milestones achieved thus far have positioned the participants and their respective organizations to make more effective and informed decisions related to crop performance, irrigation management, pest and disease monitoring, water efficiency, and drought monitoring. The distant-support period and the online symposium further contributed to the application and dissemination of the newly gained skills, ensuring a sustained impact on the institutions involved and the Kenyan agricultural sector as a whole.
